tldr: We trained a single reinforcement learning policy that enables a humanoid to perform "pivot walking"—transporting a box heavier than its arm payload by rocking it back and forth on alternating bottom corners. By distilling and fine-tuning this into an object-blind policy driven purely by an internal clock, the real Unitree G1 humanoid transported a heavy box forward by over 1 m without any external object sensors.
hero_caption: A real Unitree G1 humanoid transports a 14.9 kg case using pivot walking. The robot tilts the box onto its bottom corners and advances by alternating yaw rotations across corners.
overview:
When humans move heavy furniture or appliances too massive to lift, we intuitively rely on pivot walking. We tilt the object onto one of its bottom corners, swing it forward, and switch back and forth. Teaching a humanoid robot to do this traditionally relied on quasi-static, contact-model planning. These approaches separated stepping from object rotation, stopping the object completely between successive turns.

This paper proposes an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that simultaneously coordinates walking, whole-body balance, dual-arm contacts, and box rocking/turning within a single unified policy. A simple "transport forward" task reward causes the robot to drag or topple the box. To solve this, the authors introduced skill rewards promoting box tilt and yaw oscillations, paired with a phase reference synchronized to the box's displacement rather than time. This progress-paced reference keeps the pivot gait stable in simulation even when a heavy box gets hung up.

For real-world deployment, the policy was fine-tuned into an "object-blind" version that removes all box state observations and follows an internal periodic clock instead. In real-robot experiments with the Unitree G1, the system achieved over 1 m of forward transport across all five trials without cameras or box sensors, repeatedly rocking and pivoting the case forward.
contributions: Integrated stepping, balance, and dual-arm box rocking into a single whole-body RL policy without contact scheduling or planned static phases.
Introduced box-level pivot skill rewards and a spatial progress-paced reference synchronized to real box displacement, preventing the dragging and toppling common with simple forward rewards.

Demonstrated direct sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving over 1 m of forward box transport across all five trials without external object sensing by fine-tuning into an object-blind, clock-driven policy.

sections.heading: Whole-body loco-manipulation and pivoting: where this work stands
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in legged reinforcement learning and humanoid manipulation to place this approach in context. Earlier pivoting studies relied on quasi-static, multi-phase planning, whereas this paper learns a continuous, coordinated single gait via reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
### Legged RL and Loco-Manipulation
Advances in reinforcement learning (RL) and massively parallel simulation have enabled robust locomotion and diverse gaits on legged robots. Recently, humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation has expanded to holding, carrying, and continuously pushing objects. However, pivot walking—resting most of the load on the ground while switching contact corners to generate propulsion—presents dynamic contact transitions far more coupled and complex than standard pushing or carrying.

### Pivoting and Nonprehensile Manipulation
Rotating an object around ground contact points without lifting it is a classic nonprehensile manipulation problem. Humanoid pivoting was explored by Yoshida et al. and Murooka et al., but their methods relied on quasi-static, contact-model plans that separated stepping from rotation with pauses between motions. In contrast, this paper requires no explicit contact schedules or stationary phases. A single whole-body policy produces stepping, balance, hand forces, and box rocking as one unified gait.

### Reward Design and State-Synchronized References
Emergent complex behaviors can sometimes arise from pure task goals, but highly non-linear, high-friction contact dynamics easily trap policies in poor local minima. Additionally, fixed temporal clocks used in locomotion RL create severe mismatches when a heavy payload lags behind schedule. Drawing inspiration from virtual constraints, this work replaces temporal clocks with a spatial reference tied directly to the box's forward displacement.

sections.heading: Moving a box beyond arm limits: task setup, inputs, and outputs
sections.summary: The task asks a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid to transport a 14.9 kg case—far exceeding its 6 kg dual-arm payload limit. Running at 50 Hz, the policy outputs 29 target joint angles without external velocity commands or stepping targets.
sections.details:
### Task Definition and Physical Setup
The robot is a Unitree G1 EDU humanoid with 29 degrees of freedom across its legs, waist, arms, and wrists. The payload is a modified freestanding hard case (0.475 m wide, 0.35 m deep, 0.82 m tall, weighing 14.9 kg). Because the G1's arm payload is only 3 kg per arm (6 kg total), lifting the 14.9 kg case off the ground is physically impossible. Dragging it flat causes high friction, wearing out surfaces and hardware. Pivoting the box onto its bottom corners to offload weight is the natural mechanical solution.

The robot starts in a crouch (nominal base height 0.765 m) with both palms on the sides of the box. The transport axis is fixed, and the robot turns the box's yaw using differential hand forces, converting rotation into forward motion. No walking velocity commands or footstep schedules are given, and hand contact with the box is sustained entirely through reward incentives rather than rigid constraints.

### Observation and Action Space
The control loop runs at 50 Hz, using low-level PD controllers to track target joint angles. The action $a_t$ consists of target joint angle offsets for all 29 joints.
During training, the Actor receives proprioceptive signals (joint positions, velocities, base angular velocity, gravity vector), the previous action, box position relative to the base, box yaw deviation from start ($\sin, \cos$), and gravity in the box frame. It also takes a 3D progress reference phase signal. The Critic receives uncorrupted, privileged full states.
For real-world deployment, the Actor is turned into an object-blind version: all box observations are removed and replaced by an internal periodic clock and the robot's own yaw change ($\sin, \cos$) since the start of walking.

### Episode Termination
Simulation episodes last 20 seconds. An episode terminates immediately if the box tilts past $40^\circ$, the robot tilts more than $35^\circ$ from vertical, or the robot's feet touch the box. Foot contact is treated as a failure because the goal is dual-arm pivoting, not kicking the box forward.

sections.heading: Skill rewards and progress-paced reference: four training stages
sections.summary: Forward rewards alone lead to box dragging. To prevent this, the authors designed skill rewards for tilting and alternating yaw swings, coupled with a spatial reference paced by the box's actual displacement. Training proceeds through four stages, culminating in an object-blind policy fine-tuned with an internal clock.
sections.details:
### Skill Rewards for Pivot Walking
Rewarding only forward velocity causes policies to get stuck dragging the box flat against the floor or pushing it over unstably. To avoid these local optima, the authors added explicit box-level skill rewards:
- Yaw Tracking Reward: In early training, an alternating target yaw reference with period $T=4\text{ s}$ guides the box using a Gaussian reward. The amplitude gradually scales up over the first 2,000 iterations.
- Tilt Reward: A constant reward is granted when the box tilt angle $\theta$ relative to gravity falls within $5^\circ \le \theta \le 28^\circ$. This stops the box from turning flat on the floor while keeping a safety margin from the $40^\circ$ toppling limit. The policy is free to choose which corner contacts the ground; combining tilt with yaw oscillations naturally yields alternating corner pivots.
- Auxiliary Rewards: Incentives maintain palm-box contact, penalize torso contact, and regularize joint torques and posture.

### Progress-Paced Reference
Temporal reference clocks suffer from a major flaw: if a heavy box catches or slows down, time keeps ticking. The required turning direction flips out of sync with the box, collapsing the gait.
To fix this, the reference phase was tied directly to forward displacement $x^{\text{box}} - x_0$. With wavelength $L=0.20\text{ m}$, target yaw alternates every $L/2 = 0.10\text{ m}$. If the box stalls, the reference halts; if it slides back, the reference rewinds.
To prevent the robot from collecting yaw rewards while standing completely still, the yaw tracking reward is multiplied by a clamped forward velocity $\min(\max(0, \dot{x}^{\text{box}}), v_{\max})$ ($v_{\max}=0.15\text{ m/s}$). Yaw tracking is only rewarded when the box is actually moving forward.

### Staged Curriculum Learning
Training runs on a GPU-parallelized simulator (mjlab based on MuJoCo Warp, 4,096 environments) using PPO across four stages:
1. Stance Pretraining (4 kg): Learn to balance in a crouch with hands on a tilted box.
2. Gait Discovery (4 kg): Introduce temporal reference and skill rewards to discover alternating yaw pivots.
3. Spatial Reference Conversion: Swap the temporal clock for the progress-paced reference.
4. Mass Curriculum: Scale box mass from 4 kg to 8 kg, 14.9 kg (real hardware match), and up to 24 kg.

### Object-Blind Fine-Tuning for Deployment
The spatial reference policy $\pi_{\text{path}}$ needs exact box pose, but the real box carries no sensors or markers. The authors fine-tuned this into an object-blind policy $\pi_{\text{hw}}$ by stripping box observations from the Actor and providing only an internal 1.4-second clock and the robot's accumulated yaw change. The Critic retains privileged simulation states (true box velocity, etc.) while domain randomization—varying mass, friction, center of mass, and PD gains—prepares the policy for real-world transfer.

sections.heading: Simulation results and real G1 trials: what worked and how far it went
sections.summary: In simulation, the robot transported a 14.9 kg box 4.12 m in 20 seconds. Contact force analysis confirmed true alternating single-corner pivoting. On the physical robot, the object-blind policy achieved over 1 m of forward transport across all five trials, replicating alternating tilts and yaw swings without external sensors.
sections.details:
### Can simple forward rewards discover pivoting?
Across six ablation runs (8 kg, 14.9 kg, 24 kg) trained purely on task forward rewards without skill rewards, none developed alternating pivot walking. Five runs collapsed into dragging the box flat with poor progress (0.18–0.33 m over 20 s). The remaining run tilted the box heavily and pushed it over repeatedly. Explicit skill rewards proved essential for exploring alternating corner gaits.

### Does the policy actually pivot on corners?
Evaluating the progress-paced policy $\pi_{\text{path}}$ on 14.9 kg in simulation across 128 initial states resulted in zero falls or terminations, averaging 4.12 m forward in 20 seconds (0.21 m/s). Episodes averaged 41.2 yaw swings, with 98.7% of forward progress achieved during active swings.
Direct ground contact force measurements under each corner revealed 34 primary support switches between left and right bottom corners over 20 seconds. For 99.5% of the time, a single corner supported over 60% of the total normal force. Corner slip accounted for only 9% of total forward travel, confirming mechanically genuine pivot walking rather than angled sliding.

### Temporal Reference vs. Spatial Reference
Comparing the 14.9 kg task under temporal versus spatial references highlighted clear differences. A 4-second clock stayed stable but was sluggish (0.84 m). Shortening the temporal clock to 1.1 seconds from scratch boosted distance but caused 963 box drops across 256 environments. The spatial reference achieved 4.12 m with zero drops, confirming that pacing the gait to box progress prevents breakdowns when heavy objects lag.

### Blind Transfer to the Physical Unitree G1
The object-blind policy $\pi_{\text{hw}}$, running on an internal 1.4-second clock without box feedback, was deployed on the physical Unitree G1 with the 14.9 kg case across five trials. Motion was verified offline using an external camera and markers.
In all five runs, the robot exhibited alternating leans (mean tilt $15^\circ$, peak $22^\circ\text{--}33^\circ$) and yaw reversals, advancing 1.02 m to 1.28 m. Each run ended between 12 and 22 seconds when base pitch exceeded a safety threshold (1.0 rad). Without box observations, small phase lags and heading drifts accumulate until the robot tips backward in a deep crouch. While steady-state long-distance transport and controlled stopping remain open challenges, the results demonstrate reliable, sensor-free physical transfer of a heavy-load pivot gait.

sections.heading: Conclusions and next steps: new ground for humanoid heavy transport
sections.summary: This study demonstrates the first humanoid policy combining walking, balance, and heavy-box pivoting into a single whole-body gait via reinforcement learning. Achieving over 1 m of sensor-free pivot transport on hardware is a major step forward, while highlighting key challenges in sustained long-range transport and controlled stopping.
sections.details:
This paper presents a reinforcement learning approach to whole-body pivot walking, allowing a humanoid to transport boxes well beyond its lifting capacity. By leveraging progress-paced spatial references and skill rewards without explicit contact schedules or pauses, the policy achieves highly stable 14.9 kg box transport in simulation.

Furthermore, transferring the gait to an object-blind policy running on an internal clock enabled the physical Unitree G1 to transport the box past 1 m across all trials with clear alternating swings. Currently, trials terminate when base pitch triggers a safety stop, likely due to unobserved yaw and phase drift between robot and box. Future extensions include closing the feedback loop using onboard sensing (tactile feedback, vision, or contact force estimation) to correct drift, enabling autonomous long-distance transport, controlled stopping, and unloading.

takeaways: Generic forward rewards cause policies to settle into inefficient dragging; explicit skill rewards are necessary to guide the policy toward physically sound pivot walking.
When manipulating heavy payloads, synchronizing reference phase to actual object displacement prevents gait collapse caused by payload lag and sticking.

Using privileged object states and progress references during training, then fine-tuning into an object-blind policy driven by proprioception and an internal clock, substantially lowers the barrier to sim-to-real transfer.
limitations: Real-world transport stops after just over 1 m (roughly 12–22 seconds) when the robot's base tilt hits safety limits; continuous long-distance transport and autonomous stopping/unloading remain unsolved.
The deployed real-robot policy receives zero box feedback, making it unable to detect or correct accumulated phase drift and yaw misalignment with the box.
Corner contact switching on the physical robot was inferred from external video rather than measured directly with force sensors; dynamic contact mechanics were verified only in simulation.
